attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own newsletter post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'any changes', the data-center example, 'eventually' and the stated premise. 'Would' is firm conditional language, so this is a scorable conditional forecast.

contract.note: Counting the Oct 2025 contractual restructuring as a qualifying change relies on the broad 'any changes' reading. His logic points to reduced interest, and the deal added $250B of Azure commitments. The outcome is unresolved under either reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI disclosure dated 2025-10-28 showing a changed partnership. At most it bears on the antecedent. It shows nothing about NVIDIA revenue, so it cannot support the outcome.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated ('eventually'). Under the broad reading the condition may be met, but nothing in the packet traces any Microsoft/OpenAI change to reduced NVIDIA orders or recognized revenue. The early-resolution rule is not met and the horizon is open, so this stays unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words. He writes the claim himself while complaining about other people's 'era of agents' talk.

semantics.note: 'Will never work' is a firm, categorical forecast. The present-tense 'don't work' part sits alongside it. Despite the ranting tone, the wording is unhedged.

contract.note: The plain reading (agents never become practically useful at multistep tasks) is ordinary for a categorical 'never'. Someone could limit 'agents' to the hyped general-purpose ones, but the speaker gave no such limit. Requiring repeated, user-verified results is a fair bar.

evidence.note: Anthropic's own account of an iterative, tool-driven agent workflow that found Firefox bugs. As developer evidence it is weak alone, but Mozilla corroborates it.

Mozilla, the user that verified the results, reports 22 bug fixes and then 271 fixes shipped in released Firefox from the AI-driven scans. That is repeated, practical, independently verified output. Dated 2026-04-21.
Production study finds reliability limits and heavy human involvement. It narrows any broad conclusion but does not show agents never work.

reviews.rationale: The early-resolution rule is met. Mozilla independently confirms repeated useful multistep agent work that led to hundreds of shipped vulnerability fixes before the evaluation date. That contradicts the categorical 'will never work'. e3's reliability limits do not save a 'never' claim. The present-tense part about July 2025 is not settled by this evidence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps the antecedent and the 35% premise. It drops 'making them rely on their own AI trade stories', a minor omission. It also bundles a historical premise with the conditional forecast.

contract.note: Requiring a meaningful growth setback, and transmission attributable to it, is an ordinary reading. Severity, time window and number of affected firms are not specified, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: Aug 2025 small data-center miss with guidance in line with expectations. A candidate trigger, but it does not establish that the growth story stumbled.
Peers rose while NVIDIA dipped, and investors saw AI demand as confirmed. This argues against treating the event as a qualifying stumble. It does not test the forecast.

reviews.rationale: The antecedent, an NVIDIA growth-story stumble, is not shown to have happened. The only candidate was a minor miss that investors read as positive. With the antecedent unknown, the conditional is not scored. The 35% dependence premise also lacks matching evidence. No deadline was stated.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, about OpenAI's ChatGPT agent.

semantics.note: 'Works very very poorly and inconsistently' is a firm observation. 'Likely very expensive' is hedged, so the cost part is not scored. The proposition keeps the hedge ('probably').

contract.note: Limiting the claim to the launch version (Jul 17–21, 2025) and reading it as frequent failure on ordinary advertised tasks is fair and ordinary. Correctly, the hedged cost claim is not treated as firm.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch disclosure admits mistakes and shows partial benchmark scores. These are company tests, not representative independent reliability evidence.
A single TechRadar trial that succeeded with user help. Mildly weighs against 'very poorly', but one trial cannot establish consistency or a failure rate.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative independent repeated-task evaluation of the launch version. One company benchmark and one successful trial cannot settle whether it worked 'very very poorly and inconsistently'. The cost part is hedged ('likely') and so is not adjudicable.
